cells.tense: Right now you're holding the shape of this, and holding it well.
cells.ask: With both things going at once, take the one closest to finished and end it today — say it's done, out loud or in writing. You'll get to feel completion before you hand anything on.
cells.core:
You have two things running at the same time, and you're not picking between them. Each gets what it needs from you, and that steady attention is the work itself. Going well here isn't perfect control — it's care that doesn't run out.

The cost is quiet. Holding both so carefully means neither one gets to be finished in front of you, and the ending stays somewhere ahead. Ending one of them, plainly, would let the release follow the completion the way it's meant to. It won't settle the other one. It'll give you the small fact of one thing done, and something to set down.

cells.tense: You're already living in the version where it's all handled, and it hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick the one outcome you want most. Write what finished actually looks like — one sentence, concrete, no steps. That's aiming instead of bracing, and you'll know the difference when you read it back.
cells.core:
You've got a picture of how this should go, and you're moving toward it faster than the thing itself can. The structures you're building aren't for what's here — they're for what you're afraid will be here if you don't get ahead of it. That's the whole shape of it, and it's tiring.

Get it right and you build what the moment needs: a rough scaffold, changed when the wood warps, keeping something alive rather than pinning it. You can't build the next step before the ground's ready. One clear picture of the finished thing, drawn from what you've actually been through, gives you something to aim at instead of dozens of half-done ones to fear.

cells.tense: You set the frame once, and you've been standing outside it since.
cells.ask: Take the smallest piece of this — one drawer, one file, one shelf — and put it in order today. Just that one piece. Finishing it, even small, leaves you something that no longer needs your attention.
cells.core:
You have a sense of how things should be arranged, and you're not using it. The structure here — the patterns, the way things get kept — is running without you at the desk. You still notice when something's off. You don't move to adjust it, and things drift.

At its best it isn't grand: open the drawer, set it right, close it, think nothing more about it. That's the whole move. One small piece brought under your hand gives you back the feel of being the one who keeps things in order, and it's a feeling you can build on rather than a mood you wait for.

cells.tense: You're already setting the pattern here, and in your own account of it, it's just how things run.
cells.ask: Pick one structure you've built — a recurring agreement, an arrangement, something that keeps happening because you set it up — and name it out loud to whoever lives inside it as yours. One sentence, plain, no apology.
cells.core:
You've been the one deciding what holds and what gets kept, and you describe it as if it simply ran. The frames other people move inside are frames you made, and you don't talk about them as choices you made — so you can't revise them and no one can thank you for them.

Done honestly, a structure you set holds, and when the thing is finished you let it finish without holding on. That letting-go is what completion is for — not defeat, the reward. One arrangement, said as yours, to the person who lives inside it. The words are the acknowledgment. They only have to be true.
